paragraphs.text: Stickler syndrome type VI is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in COL9A3. Its consistent features are moderate-to-profound progressive sensorineural hearing loss and moderate to high myopia with vitreoretinal degeneration. Retinal detachment and cataract occur occasionally. Skeletal involvement is more variable and can include spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia and early-onset arthropathy (Markova et al., 2021; Rad et al., 2022).

paragraphs.text: Hanson-Kahn et al. (2018) reported a 12-year-old boy of Indian ancestry (family R08-308) whose parents were third cousins. He failed his newborn hearing screen and had moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss with mild enlargement of the vestibular aqueducts. His speech delay was attributed to the hearing loss. He had progressive high myopia but no vitreous abnormalities or retinal degeneration. Femoral and tibial bowing were noted at birth. Radiographs at 6 years showed slightly flattened proximal femoral epiphyses, normal knee epiphyses, and mild platyspondyly. Other radiographic findings were irregular vertebral endplates, flattened acetabula, and irregularity of the medial distal femoral epiphyses. He had midfacial hypoplasia and did not have cleft palate or pes planus. He also had autoimmune hypothyroidism. His intelligence was normal and his growth parameters were in the normal range.

All 6 patients were highly myopic, with congenital megalophthalmos and abnormal, hypoplastic vitreous gel, and all had sensorineural hearing loss. One of the 6 patients had severe arthropathy. Nixon et al. (2019) noted that sensorineural hearing loss is more common and more severe in recessive than in dominant Stickler syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Markova et al. (2021) reported a 3-year-old Russian boy born to nonconsanguineous parents. He had congenital high bilateral myopia, hip dysplasia, and grade 3-4 bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with delayed speech development. On ophthalmologic examination he had peripheral retinal pigment rearrangement with dystrophic foci, vitreous floaters, and a preretinal membrane. His electroretinogram was normal and he had no retinal detachment. Radiography showed mild spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, including mild platyspondyly, kyphosis, flattened and irregular femoral heads, coxa valga, and flattened distal femoral epiphyses. He also had spina bifida occulta of the sacral vertebrae. Other findings were genu valgum, a waddling gait, early-onset arthropathy with lower limb joint pain, lumbar lordosis, limited hip abduction, prominent knee joints, long fingers, and planovalgus foot deformity. His facial features included a flattened nasal bridge, small nose, mild midface hypoplasia, and high palate, without cleft palate. His height was normal.

paragraphs.text: Rad et al. (2022) reported 5 patients from 3 unrelated consanguineous Iranian families. In family 1, the patient was a 28-year-old woman. She was the oldest and only affected of 3 children born to first-cousin parents. She had high myopia in both eyes, vitreoretinal degeneration with empty vitreous, multiple lattice degenerations, retinal pigmentary changes, and severe progressive sensorineural hearing loss. Her skull x-ray showed unilateral absence of the frontal sinus. She also had knee pain, pes planus, low-set ears, short metacarpals with widened epiphyses, mild platyspondyly of the thoracic spine, and genu valgum. She did not have cleft palate, micrognathia, short stature, retinal detachment, or intellectual disability.

paragraphs.text: Family 3 of Rad et al. (2022) had 2 affected and 2 healthy children born to first-cousin parents. The affected children were an 11.8-year-old boy and a 3.1-year-old girl. Both had myopia and congenital moderate to severe progressive sensorineural hearing impairment. In both, x-ray and detailed examination showed spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia. Both also had pes planus, a depressed nasal bridge, and anteverted nares. Midface hypoplasia and downslanting palpebral fissures were more pronounced in the girl. The boy reported knee pain, especially when running. He also had genu valgum, bowed tibiae, short metacarpals, a broad hallux, irregular femoral epiphyses, and flat acetabular roofs with flattened femoral heads. Neither child had cleft palate, and none of the individuals in the study showed signs of intellectual disability.
